overview:
Iraq's army crossed into Kuwait before dawn on 2 August 1990 and had the emirate under control within a day. Saddam Hussein's government had emerged from eight years of war with Iran deep in debt, much of it owed to Kuwait, and blamed its neighbour for depressing oil prices by overproducing and for drawing crude from the shared Rumaila field; older Iraqi claims that Kuwait was rightfully a province gave the seizure a nationalist frame. The fighting inside Kuwait was brief but not nominal. The emir's guard held out at Dasman Palace long enough for the ruling family to flee to Saudi Arabia, Kuwaiti armoured units fought a delaying action at the Al-Jahra bridges, and there was resistance on Failaka island. Then came seven months of occupation, looting, and detentions that emptied the country of much of its population.

The response was unusually broad because the Cold War was ending: the Soviet Union did not shield Baghdad, and the UN Security Council moved quickly to demand withdrawal, impose sanctions, and eventually authorise force if Iraq did not leave by 15 January 1991. A coalition that eventually numbered dozens of states — including Egypt, Syria and Saudi Arabia alongside the United States, Britain and France — assembled in the Saudi desert under Operation Desert Shield. The air campaign opened on 17 January and ran for five weeks, dismantling Iraqi command networks, power and bridges while Iraq fired Scud missiles at Israel and Saudi Arabia in a largely unsuccessful attempt to split the alliance. Iraq's one significant offensive move, a thrust into the Saudi border town of Khafji at the end of January, was thrown back. The precision-strike narrative broke down on 13 February, when two bombs punched into a public shelter in Baghdad's Amiriyah district and killed at least 408 civilians; American officials insisted it was a command bunker, a claim outside investigators have never substantiated.

The ground war began on 24 February and was over in a hundred hours. While marines and Arab forces pushed straight into Kuwait, US and British armoured divisions swung far to the west and hooked east into the Republican Guard. The engagements the dataset records — 73 Easting, Medina Ridge, Al Busayyah, Jalibah airfield, Wadi al-Batin, Rumaila — were mostly one-sided: thermal sights, longer-ranged guns and total air supremacy let coalition tanks kill Iraqi armour before it could see them. Some of the worst coalition losses came from friendly fire, as at Phase Line Bullet. Retreating Iraqi columns were pounded on the road north from Kuwait City, and images of that wreckage helped push Washington toward a ceasefire on 28 February with Saddam still in power. Kuwait was restored, but hundreds of oil wells burned for months, and the Shia and Kurdish uprisings that followed the ceasefire were crushed while coalition forces stood by.
significance: The war set the template for how the United States fought and justified war for the next two decades: a UN mandate, a paying coalition, an overwhelming air campaign, and a ground phase that ended before the political questions were settled. It showcased a generation of weapons — stealth aircraft, laser-guided bombs, thermal-sighted tanks, satellite navigation — and made "precision" a public argument about legitimacy as much as a technical claim, even as Amiriyah showed its limits. It also left everything unfinished. Saddam survived, sanctions and no-fly zones ground on through the 1990s at enormous cost to Iraqi civilians, the permanent American military presence in Saudi Arabia became a rallying grievance for al-Qaeda, and the sense that the job had been left half-done shaped the case for invading Iraq again in 2003.
coverage: Written from the Wikipedia and Britannica overviews, the US State Department historian's account of the diplomacy, and the record of the Amiriyah bombing; the dataset's thirteen events are almost entirely set-piece battles, which skews toward the coalition's own operational history and away from the seven-month occupation of Kuwait, the air war, and the postwar uprisings. The largest gap is Iraqi casualties: estimates of military dead range from roughly 20,000 to 50,000 and civilian estimates vary by an order of magnitude, because no independent count was made and both Baghdad's figures and early US wartime reporting were shaped by propaganda — the fabricated Kuwaiti "incubator" testimony being the best-known instance.
